lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Hi everyone, good to see you. Welcome to the first real class of Module A.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Last time we talked about the paper. Today we finally start the subject. No calculator needed today, I promise.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Quick question first. When the rupee falls against the dollar, who decides that?

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Most people have a vague answer. R-B-I, the government, the market, someone. But I-I-B-F likes this area. Questions on what moves exchange rates, and on settlement dates, both show up in the papers we checked.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: And everything in Module A, every rate and every sum, sits on top of today's picture. So today is the foundation. No heavy theory, I'll keep it simple. Stay with me, okay?

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Picture a branch counter, eleven in the morning. A customer comes back with yesterday's receipt in his hand.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: He says, "Yesterday you gave me dollars at eighty-five twenty. Today your board says eighty-five sixty-five. Who changed it? R-B-I?"

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Fair question, right?

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Now I know what many of you are thinking. R-B-I fixes the rupee rate every morning, and banks just follow. And a few of you are thinking the opposite. Each bank decides its own rate, any rate it likes.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: So which one is it? Lock your answer.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Okay. Here's the honest answer. Neither. We'll see why by the end. First, one word needs to be clear. What is foreign exchange?

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: The law for this is FEMA, the Foreign Exchange Management Act of nineteen ninety-nine. It came into force in June two thousand, replacing the old FERA.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: FEMA first defines foreign currency simply. Any currency other than Indian currency. Dollar, euro, yen, dirham, all foreign currency.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Then it defines foreign exchange, and this is wider. Foreign exchange means foreign currency, and it includes three more things. Think of them as three pockets.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Pocket one: deposits, credits and balances payable in a foreign currency. Like an exporter's dollar account.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Pocket two: drafts, travellers cheques, letters of credit or bills drawn in rupees, but payable in a foreign currency.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Pocket three is the surprise. The same kinds of paper, drawn by someone outside India, but payable in rupees.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Read that third one again. Payable in rupees, and still foreign exchange, because it's drawn from outside India. Examiners love that line.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: So the hook is simple. Foreign currency is the money itself. Foreign exchange adds the deposits and papers in those three pockets.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: And the exchange rate is just the price of one currency in another. In India we quote it directly: so many rupees for one dollar.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: An importer paying dollars wants a strong rupee. An exporter receiving dollars likes a weaker one. Same rate, opposite feelings. Okay, first chapter done. Stretch for a second.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Now, where is this market? Here's the first surprise. There's no building.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: The forex market is over the counter, O-T-C. Careful, that's not our branch counter. It just means there's no exchange in the middle. Banks and dealers deal with each other directly, mostly on screens.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: And it follows the sun. The day starts in Sydney and Tokyo and ends in New York. So somewhere it's open round the clock on weekdays.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: In India, the normal market hours for rupee deals are nine in the morning to five in the evening. And Saturday is not a working day for forex.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Now, who's trading? The central bank, for its reserves and to steady the market. Banks, for their customers and their own trading.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Companies, for trade, and to protect themselves from rate changes. Investors and funds. Brokers who bring buyers and sellers together. And individuals.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Their reasons boil down to five. Trade, investment, hedging, speculation, and arbitrage. Hedging means protecting yourself from a rate change. Speculation means taking a risk to profit from one.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Arbitrage gets one card. Buy where it's cheap, sell where it's dear, at the same moment. With two currencies or two centres, it's simple arbitrage. With three or more, like rupee to dollar to euro and back, it's compound.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: And because arbitrageurs jump on every gap, prices in different centres stay close.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Next, the two tiers. Banks dealing with each other is the interbank market, the wholesale side. A bank dealing with you is the merchant market, and merchant here means any customer. Merchant rates are built on interbank rates, with the bank's margin built in.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Everyone with me? Good. Now a part that's asked as a straight question. When is a deal settled? The day the money actually changes hands is called the value date.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: FEDAI, the banks' own association that frames the rules for forex dealing, gives four names. Cash or ready, settled the same day. Tom, short for tomorrow, settled the next working day. Spot, settled on the second working day after the deal. And forward, anything beyond spot.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Spot is the market's base rate. A dealer's quote is a spot rate unless it says otherwise. And a one-month forward is counted from the spot date, not from today.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Now be careful, this is where people slip. Spot does not mean today. Spot means the second working day, so weekends and holidays are simply skipped. A Monday deal with Wednesday a holiday settles on Thursday.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Still with me? One more date rule, for a customer's forward contract. If its delivery date turns out to be a holiday known at least three working days ahead, deliver on the working day before. If the holiday is sudden, deliver on the next working day.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: So for forward delivery: known early, go back. Sudden, go forward. That's chapter two. Deep breath.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Okay, back to our customer. Why was the dollar dearer today?

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: A see-saw. On one side, people who want dollars. Importers paying bills, students paying fees, investors pulling money out. On the other side, people who have dollars to sell. Exporters, money sent home from abroad, investors bringing money in.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: When more people want dollars than offer them, the dollar side goes heavy. The rupee weakens. When dollars pour in, the rupee strengthens. That's the whole engine.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: See, the rate is rupees for one dollar. If you need more rupees for one dollar, the rupee has become weaker. So our customer's eighty-five sixty-five means the rupee fell a little overnight.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Now, a thirty-second refresher from J-A-I-I-B. The balance of payments is India's account book with the rest of the world.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: The current account holds trade, services, income, and money sent home by Indians abroad. The capital account holds investment and loans coming in and going out. And no, this current account is not the one at your branch.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: So what pushes the see-saw? The factors fall into three groups. Fundamental, technical, and speculative.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Fundamental factors are the economy itself. A big current account deficit means India spends more abroad than it earns, so the rupee weakens. Inflation higher here than abroad weakens it. Higher interest rates pull money in and strengthen it. Then growth, the government's finances, foreign investment, and political stability.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Technical factors are about how the market is set up. Government controls, limits on capital moving in and out, and the demand and supply sitting in the market that day. And speculative factors are expectations. If traders expect the dollar to rise, they buy it, and it rises.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Quick check. Some of you are thinking, if inflation in India runs higher than in the U-S, the rupee gets stronger. Others are thinking it gets weaker. Which is it?

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Weaker. If the same basket of goods gets dearer faster in India than in the U-S, each rupee buys less. So over time, it's worth less against the dollar. That idea has a name, purchasing power parity. You only need the idea today.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: One more idea. Interest rate parity, and it's about the price for a future date. If a currency's price for a future date is lower than today's, that currency is at a forward discount. If higher, it's at a forward premium.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: The rule: the currency with the higher interest rate trades at a forward discount. And if the rupee is at a discount, the dollar is at a premium.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Don't mix this with the see-saw. Higher rates pull money in and lift a currency today. Parity is only about the forward price. The sums come in A-zero-five.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Inflation and the forward discount are classic traps, and now you won't fall for them. Chapter three, done.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Now the big question from the start. Does R-B-I fix the rate?

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: First, the regimes. A fixed rate is set officially, and the central bank holds it there. A floating rate is set purely by the market. And a managed float is in between: the market sets it, the central bank smooths it, with no fixed target.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: And mind two words. An official cut in a fixed rate is a devaluation. A market fall in a floating rate is a depreciation, and a rise is an appreciation.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: India started with a par value system, a fixed official rate, under the Bretton Woods system after the Second World War. When that system broke down in nineteen seventy-one, the rupee was linked to the pound sterling.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: From September nineteen seventy-five, it was pegged to a basket of currencies, so no single currency could pull it around.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Then came the crisis of nineteen ninety-one. In July, the rupee was devalued in two steps, about eighteen percent in all.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: In March nineteen ninety-two came the Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System, LERMS. A dual rate: forty percent of exchange earnings at the official rate, sixty percent at the market rate.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: And in March nineteen ninety-three, the two rates were unified. From then, the rupee's rate is market determined. In August nineteen ninety-four, the rupee became convertible on the current account, as India accepted Article Eight of the I-M-F.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Convertible on the current account means you can change rupees into dollars for trade, services or travel without special permission. Only a short list is banned or capped by the rules. Capital moves still have limits.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: So what does R-B-I do today? It doesn't fix the rate. India runs a managed float. In R-B-I's own words, it acts to keep the market orderly and contain excessive volatility. It buys or sells dollars from its reserves when the swings get jerky.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: And the reference rate you see every afternoon? It's published by F-B-I-L, Financial Benchmarks India, since July twenty eighteen.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: It's built from real spot trades in a random fifteen-minute slot, between eleven-thirty and twelve-thirty, around midday. It comes out at about one-thirty in the afternoon.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: It's a benchmark, used for things like converting figures in reports. It isn't a rate that R-B-I forces on your deal. Your counter rate comes from the interbank rate, with your bank's margin built in.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: So, back to our customer. What's the one-line answer? The rate moves with the market every day. R-B-I only steps in to stop wild swings, and our board follows the interbank rate.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Okay, pause the video now, and answer three questions. One. A deal is struck on Monday for spot. When is it settled, if there's no holiday? Two. Which of these strengthens the rupee: a bigger current account deficit, higher inflation in India than abroad, or more foreign investment coming in? Three. Since when has the rupee's rate been market determined?

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Answers. One, Wednesday, the second working day. Two, more foreign investment coming in. The other two weaken it. Three, March nineteen ninety-three, when the dual rates were unified. Got all three? Well done.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Now let's read the map we built. The market behind the counter. What forex is: the money, plus every claim in the three pockets. The players and their five motives. Deal dates: cash, tom, spot, forward. Three groups of factors pushing one see-saw. And regimes: from par value to a managed float, with R-B-I steadying, not fixing.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Small homework. Draw the see-saw tonight, and put three factors on it, each on the side it pushes. Two minutes, that's all.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: And next class, we walk up to the counter itself. I'll ask you one question that trips up a lot of people. At a forex counter, is the bank buying, or selling?

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: That's our class for today. Take care of yourselves, and I'll see you in the next one.
